newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE denies request for recount in Bosnian election.
newsitem.headline: OSCE denies request for recount in Bosnian election.

text.p: The final authority for Bosnia's post-war elections on Friday rejected a recommendation from its own appeals body for a complete recount of votes in national polling on September 14.

Friday's decision apparently cleared the way for final certification of the election results and installation of various new government bodies created under the provisions of last December's Dayton peace agreement.

"The Provisional Election Commission is of the unanimous opinion that an additional physical recount of all ballots...is neither a practical nor a necessary response to the concerns raised," its official decision read on Friday.
The Provisional Election Commission (PEC) was established by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE), charged by Dayton with conducting Bosnia's post-war elections.
The PEC's own Election Appeals Sub-Commission on Friday had called for a recount based on the suspiciously high number of ballots cast in the September 14 voting.
"The PEC was told that it would have taken a hundred people about two weeks to recount the ballots and they (PEC) decided it just wasn't necessary," Nicole Szulc, an OSCE spokeswoman, told Reuters.
"It would have delayed certification of the final results and delayed installation of the new government too."
The PEC announced that a series of recalculations had been carried out on the ballots and that minor discrepancies had been corrected without any change in final results.
The PEC includes representation from Bosnia's Moslem, Serb and Croat communities and is chaired by Ambassador Robert Frowick, an American, who heads the OSCE mission in Bosnia.
Frowick later issued a statement saying the discrepancy in the turnout rate stemmed from a technical mistake by OSCE staff.
The OSCE relied on a total of 2.9 million voters based on a U.N. document "that focused on refugees, not voters per se," instead of 3.25 million according to the 1991 census, he said.
"I take full responsibility for the Missions's mistake initially basing its calculation on this manifest under-estimation of the number of eligible voters," he said.
Some 2,4 million people actually voted at the elections, he said.
"The Elections Appeals Sub-Commission will meet on Saturday and we expect they will accept the decision and surrender jursidictions as requested," OSCE spokeswoman Szulc said.
Frowick would then be free to certify the results, after which the new institutions of government could be formed.

Bosnians voted on September 14 for a three-man national presidency, a national House of Representatives, separate parliaments for the Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic, a Serb republic president and cantonal assemblies.
Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem, was the winner of the chairmanship of the collective presidency by 41,000 votes based on preliminary final results announced by OSCE earlier this week.
